mcqs.question: Why does the two-heap median trick use a max-heap for the lower half of values and a min-heap for the upper half, rather than the reverse?
options: Each heap type is chosen so its root is exactly the element closest to the median — the max-heap's root is the lower half's largest value, and the min-heap's root is the upper half's smallest value
A max-heap always sorts faster than a min-heap for small datasets
The choice is arbitrary and could be swapped with no effect
Min-heaps cannot store the smaller half of a dataset
mcqs.explanation: The values needed at O(1) access are specifically the boundary values nearest the median from each side, and a max-heap's root is its largest element while a min-heap's root is its smallest — exactly matching what's needed from the lower and upper halves respectively. Swapping the heap types would put the wrong boundary values at the roots, breaking O(1) median access, and this has nothing to do with sorting speed or a heap type's ability to store any particular range of values.

mcqs.question: The two-heap median finder maintains two invariants after every insert. What would break if only the size-balance invariant were maintained, without also maintaining the ordering invariant (lower-half max ≤ upper-half min)?
options: Nothing — size balance alone is sufficient to guarantee a correct median
The heaps would no longer support insertion at all
A value could end up in the wrong half relative to the true median, so even though the heaps are equal-sized, the roots wouldn't actually represent the correct median boundary
The time complexity of insert would become O(n)
mcqs.explanation: Size balance alone only guarantees the heaps split the data evenly by count, not that every value in the max-heap is actually less than every value in the min-heap — without that ordering guarantee, the roots could reflect an incorrect split point, giving a wrong median despite technically balanced sizes. Insertion still works mechanically without the ordering invariant; it just produces wrong answers, and this doesn't change insert's time complexity.

mcqs.question: An insert implementation pushes directly into whichever heap 'seems right' based on comparing against the current median, but never performs the transfer-through-the-other-heap step. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing — comparing against the current median is sufficient to place a value correctly
The size invariant, the ordering invariant, or both can silently break, causing find_median() to return a wrong value with no error raised
The heaps will throw a runtime exception on the very next insert
This only fails when the incoming value is negative
mcqs.explanation: Skipping the transfer step means neither invariant is actively enforced on every insert — a value can land in a heap that grows the size imbalance beyond one element, or land on the wrong side of the true boundary if the comparison uses a stale root — and both failures are silent, since find_median() just reads whatever happens to be at the roots without validating them. No heap operation here throws on this kind of misplacement, and the bug is unrelated to whether the incoming value is negative.

mcqs.question: Why does the two-heap approach beat an augmented BST for median-finding specifically, even though both achieve O(log n) insert?
options: The two-heap approach reads the median in true O(1), with no traversal, while even an augmented BST typically needs to walk toward the middle or rely on stored subtree sizes to locate it
Augmented BSTs cannot support O(log n) insertion
The two-heap approach supports arbitrary rank queries, which a BST cannot
Two heaps use strictly less memory than any BST implementation
mcqs.explanation: The two-heap approach's real advantage is median-read speed: the median is always sitting at one or both heap roots, a plain O(1) peek, whereas even a size-augmented BST needs some additional traversal or size-lookup logic to locate the middle. Augmented BSTs do support O(log n) insertion, they're actually the structure that supports arbitrary rank/percentile queries (which two heaps cannot), and memory usage isn't inherently lower for heaps versus BSTs in general.

mcqs.question: Extending the two-heap median trick to a sliding window of the last k elements requires removal of arbitrary elements. Why does this break the simple two-heap approach?
options: A heap only supports efficient removal of its root, not an arbitrary element buried inside it, and the evicted element is rarely at the root
Heaps cannot store more than k elements at once
Sliding windows always require converting the heap into a sorted array first
The size-balance invariant becomes impossible to define for a sliding window
mcqs.explanation: The element that ages out of the window is essentially arbitrary from the heap's perspective and generally isn't sitting at the root, and a standard heap has no efficient way to locate or remove a non-root element — only extract-root is fast. There's no fixed capacity limit forcing this, no need to convert to a sorted array, and the size-balance invariant is still well-defined; it's the removal mechanism that's the actual obstacle, addressed via lazy deletion.
